summary: You ended with the canonical one-pass hash map solution and passed all tests. The main gap was early problem-solving momentum: you started with an O(n^2) double loop and needed multiple hints to pivot to the complement+hash map approach. Once prompted, you implemented the optimized approach cleanly and articulated correct complexity.

test_results.summary_note: All visible and hidden tests passed; no failures.

dimensions.name: Correctness & Completeness
dimensions.label: strong
dimensions.what_went_well: Returned correct indices and avoided using the same element twice by checking the complement before inserting the current element. Handled duplicates correctly (e.g., [3,3] target 6) because you store prior index then match on the second occurrence.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Minor: returning [] is fine given the prompt says exactly one valid answer exists; in real interview settings you can omit the fallback or raise/assert to align with guarantees.

dimensions.name: Problem-Solving & Thinking
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: You recognized the brute-force double loop felt slow under constraints and were open to changing approach. Once the complement idea clicked, you quickly rewrote the solution correctly.
dimensions.what_to_improve: You got stuck on how to leverage a hash-based structure until guided; aim to more quickly derive the invariant: "for each x, I need to know if (target-x) appeared earlier".

dimensions.name: Technical Communication
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: You verbalized your initial approach, flagged performance concerns, and confirmed final complexity clearly: O(n) time and O(n) space.
dimensions.what_to_improve: When considering a set/dict, you said you weren’t sure what you’d look up; practice explicitly stating the lookup goal (the complement) and the stored information (value -> index) earlier, which makes the transition to the optimal solution more self-driven.

dimensions.name: Complexity & Optimization
dimensions.label: strong
dimensions.what_went_well: Final solution matches expected optimal complexity for the problem: O(n) time with a hash map and O(n) additional space. You correctly stated both.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Build the habit of doing a quick constraints check up front (n up to 1e5) to immediately rule out O(n^2) without needing to "feel" it’s slow.

dimensions.name: Code Quality
dimensions.label: strong
dimensions.what_went_well: Code is concise and idiomatic Python: clear variable naming (seen, complement), single pass, and correct ordering of operations (check then insert).
dimensions.what_to_improve: Consider adding a brief comment about why you check before insert (prevents using same index twice) if writing for readability in collaborative codebases.

dimensions.name: Independence
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: You incorporated hints effectively and quickly converted them into a correct implementation.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Work on generating the complement-hashmap pattern without prompting; this is a very common template problem and should become an immediate recall pattern.

thinking_and_logic: You initially pursued brute force (checking every pair), then recognized it wouldn’t scale. With guidance, you reframed the task as: while scanning left-to-right, maintain a map from value to index for all prior elements; for each current value n at index i, check if target-n exists already, and if so return the stored index and i. The key correctness detail is checking before inserting the current element, which prevents reusing the same element twice and naturally supports duplicates.
code_assessment: Your final implementation is the standard correct approach: a dictionary for O(1) average membership checks, returning indices in the required form, and storing indices to preserve original positions (avoiding the common sorting pitfall). Test results confirm full correctness across visible and hidden cases.

next_steps.action: Practice deriving the complement-hashmap approach from first principles on similar problems
next_steps.why: You needed hints to move from O(n^2) to O(n); building recall and derivation speed is key for interviews.
next_steps.how: Do 8–10 variants: Two Sum, Two Sum II (sorted), 3Sum (reduce to Two Sum), Subarray Sum Equals K, Contains Duplicate, and "pair with difference k". For each, write the invariant in one sentence before coding: "store X so I can query Y in O(1)".

next_steps.action: Add a constraints-first checkpoint before committing to an approach
next_steps.why: It helps you reject non-viable complexities early and shows strong interview instincts.
next_steps.how: In the first minute, translate constraints to an upper bound: n=1e5 implies O(n^2)=1e10 ops (too big), so target O(n log n) or O(n). Say that out loud, then pick data structures accordingly.

next_steps.action: Drill “what am I looking up?” as a standard question when considering hash structures
next_steps.why: You hesitated when you suggested set/dict; the missing piece was defining the lookup target (complement).
next_steps.how: When you think "hash map", immediately answer: key=?, value=?, and query=?; e.g., key=value seen, value=index, query=complement.

patterns_to_study: single-pass scan with state (store previous elements)
encouragement: Once you had the right framing, you executed quickly and correctly—focus now on making that framing automatic so you can reach the optimal approach without external prompts.

transcript.text: Here's the problem: given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target.
Okay, I'll loop through every pair and check the sums. Writing that now.
Hmm, this feels slow but I'm not sure how to make it faster. I'm a bit stuck on how to avoid the double loop.
Think about what kind of data structure gives you fast lookups.
A set? Or a dictionary... I'm not sure what I'd look up though.
As you walk the array, consider storing the values you've already seen along with their indices.
Okay so I keep a dictionary of value to index. But I still don't see how that finds the pair.
For each element, before inserting it, check whether target minus the current value is already in your dictionary.
Oh! Right, the complement. Okay, rewriting it with the dictionary now.
Done, running the tests... they pass.
One loop, so O(n) time, and O(n) space for the dictionary.
That's time. Let's wrap up here.
